title: Circulatory and immune systems
summary: The heart, blood vessels, blood, lymph and the body's lines of defense.
cards.0.p: The heart is a pump made of cardiac muscle. It has two atria at the top and two ventricles at the bottom. Valves keep blood flowing in one direction. There is a tricuspid valve on the right side and a bicuspid valve on the left.
cards.0.svg#0: the right half of the heart is drawn on the left
cards.0.svg#14: the septum keeps right and left blood from mixing
cards.0.key: Semilunar valves sit where the arteries leave the heart. The left ventricle has the thickest wall, because it pumps blood to the whole body.
cards.1.p: The heart makes its own signal to contract. The SA node starts the signal, and the AV node holds it briefly and passes it to the ventricles. Contraction is called systole, and relaxing and filling with blood is called diastole. One cycle takes about 0.8 seconds.
cards.1.key: The SA node is in the right atrium. The signal spreads through the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibers. Sympathetic nerves speed up the heart, and parasympathetic nerves slow it down.
cards.2.p: In pulmonary circulation, blood goes from the right ventricle to the lungs, picks up oxygen and returns to the left atrium. In systemic circulation, blood goes from the left ventricle through the aorta to the tissues, drops off its oxygen and returns to the right atrium.
cards.2.key: Blood returns to the heart from the lungs through the pulmonary veins, and from the tissues through the superior and inferior venae cavae. Vessels are named by the direction of blood flow.
cards.3.h: Blood vessels, pulse and blood pressure
cards.3.p: An artery carries blood away from the heart. Its elastic wall stretches with every beat, and this stretch is called the pulse. A vein brings blood back to the heart, has low pressure and has valves. The wall of a capillary is one cell thick.
cards.3.svg#7: pulse: the wave in an artery
cards.3.key: Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg. The larger number shows systole, and the smaller number shows diastole. The muscles around the veins push the blood in them toward the heart.
cards.3.once.soru: Which vessel do you count your pulse from at your wrist?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: The artery wall stretches with every beat. You feel this wave with your finger.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The pressure in a vein is low, so no pulse can be felt.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Capillaries are so thin that no pulse can be taken from them.
cards.4.p: Blood flows slowest in the capillaries. At the arterial end of a capillary, blood pressure wins, so water and small molecules filter into the tissue. At the venous end, osmotic pressure pulls the water back.
cards.4.key: O₂ and CO₂ cross by diffusion. The small amount of fluid that does not return to the blood is collected by lymph capillaries.
cards.5.p: Tissue fluid that does not return to the blood enters the lymph capillaries and is then called lymph. Lymph joins the blood at the subclavian vein. Lymph nodes filter microbes out of the lymph.
cards.5.svg#8: fats absorbed in the small intestine also enter the lymph
cards.5.key: Lymph circulation does not form a loop and has no pump. The spleen, thymus and tonsils are also lymphatic organs.
cards.5.once.soru: When your throat is infected, why do the glands under your jaw swell?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Lymph nodes filter out microbes. Lymphocytes multiply there and the node swells.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The swollen structures are lymph nodes, not blood vessels.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The swollen glands are lymph nodes, not salivary glands.
cards.6.p: About 55% of blood is plasma. Plasma holds water, proteins, ions and nutrients. Red blood cells carry oxygen with hemoglobin, white blood cells defend the body, and platelets start clotting.
cards.6.svg#21: white cell types: neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil (granular),
cards.6.svg#22: monocyte (becomes a macrophage in tissue), lymphocyte (agranular)
cards.6.svg#23: all blood cells are made in red bone marrow
cards.6.key: Platelets are also called thrombocytes, and they are cell fragments. In mammals, mature red blood cells have no nucleus.
cards.7.p: At a wound, platelets form a plug and release thromboplastin. With the help of Ca2+, thromboplastin turns prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin, and the fibrin mesh forms the clot.
cards.7.svg#7: made in the liver with vitamin K
cards.7.key: Vitamin K is needed to make prothrombin. If vitamin K or Ca²⁺ is low, clotting is delayed.
cards.7.etk.soru: Put the steps of clotting in order.
cards.7.etk.ogeler.5: The fibrin mesh forms the clot
cards.7.once.soru: Why does blood clot at a wound and not inside the vessel?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: Thromboplastin is released from injured tissue and platelets.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: Ca²⁺ is always present in blood.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: Fibrinogen is always present in plasma, but it does not turn into fibrin without a wound.
cards.8.p: Blood type is set by the antigens on the membrane of red blood cells. Plasma holds antibodies against the antigens the person lacks. If the donor's antigen meets the recipient's antibody, the red blood cells clump.
cards.8.svg#15: Rh+: D antigen on red cells  ·  Rh−: none
cards.8.svg#16: in an Rh− person, anti-D forms only after meeting Rh+ blood
cards.8.key: In an Rh− person, anti-D antibodies form after meeting Rh+ blood. If an Rh− mother carries an Rh+ baby, Rh incompatibility can occur. For red blood cells, O Rh− is the universal donor.
cards.9.p: A drop of blood is mixed separately with anti-A, anti-B and anti-D sera. If the red blood cells clump in a serum, the red cells carry that antigen.
cards.9.svg#20: clumps = agglutination (+) · smooth color = no agglutination (−)
cards.9.key: If there is clumping in both anti-A and anti-B sera, the blood type is AB. If there is clumping in neither, the blood type is O.
cards.9.once.soru: A person's blood clumps only in anti-B serum. What is their blood type?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Clumping in anti-B serum shows the B antigen. There is no clumping in anti-D serum, so the person is Rh−.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: If the person were type A, there would be clumping in anti-A serum, and if Rh+, in anti-D serum.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: If the person were type AB, there would also be clumping in anti-A serum.
cards.10.p: Innate defense gives the same response to every microbe. The first line of defense is the skin, mucus and stomach acid. The second line includes phagocytosis, inflammation and fever.
cards.10.svg#0: the body's three lines of defense
cards.10.key: During inflammation, histamine widens the blood vessels. When a monocyte moves into tissue, it becomes a macrophage and engulfs microbes.
cards.10.once.soru: Why does a small cut on your hand turn red and swell?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The blood vessels widen and more blood and defense cells reach the area.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: A clot stops bleeding. The redness and swelling come from inflammation.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The first response at a cut comes from innate defense, not antibodies.
cards.11.p: A macrophage displays a piece of the microbe on its surface, and a helper T cell recognizes this piece. B lymphocytes release antibodies, which is called humoral immunity. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells, which is called cell-mediated immunity. In the end, memory cells remain.
cards.11.key: B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow, and T lymphocytes mature in the thymus. A B lymphocyte becomes a plasma cell and releases antibodies.
cards.11.once.soru: Which cell directly kills a cell that a virus has entered?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: A cytotoxic T cell recognizes the infected cell and destroys it directly. This is called cell-mediated immunity.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: A B lymphocyte makes antibodies, but it does not kill the cell directly.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: A red blood cell carries oxygen. It does not defend the body.
cards.12.p: In active immunity, the body makes the antibodies itself. It starts late but lasts long, and it is gained by having a disease or getting a vaccine. In passive immunity, ready-made antibodies are received. Antiserum and breast milk protect this way, and the effect starts right away but does not last long.
cards.12.svg#15: memory cells form only in active immunity
cards.12.key: A vaccine protects against a disease in advance. Antiserum helps right away during a disease or poisoning. The anti-D shot given to an Rh− mother is also passive immunity.
cards.13.p: The tissue antigens on cell membranes differ from person to person. Cytotoxic T cells recognize a transplanted organ as foreign and attack it. This is called rejection. That is why tissue matching is checked before a transplant.
cards.13.svg#9: identical twins have the same tissue antigens
cards.13.key: A suitable donor is most often found among siblings. Transplant patients are given drugs that suppress the immune system.
cards.13.once.soru: Who could be the best donor for a kidney transplant?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Tissue antigens are inherited and are the same in identical twins.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Tissue antigens vary a lot from person to person.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.yazi: Anyone with the same blood type
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: A matching blood type is not enough. Tissue antigens are checked too.
cards.14.p: An overreaction to a harmless substance is called an allergy. When the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, it is called an autoimmune disease. In AIDS, the HIV virus destroys helper T cells. A drop in hemoglobin in the blood is called anemia.
cards.14.svg#4: risk of heart attack and stroke
cards.14.key: In an allergy, IgE antibodies are made at the first contact, and symptoms appear at later contacts. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease. Atherosclerosis is the buildup of fatty plaque in the vessel wall.
cards.14.once.soru: In a pollen allergy, which substance causes the itching and swelling?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: Mast cells release histamine. The vessels widen and itching starts.
cards.15.p:
• The heart has four chambers, and the SA node starts the signal to contract.
• Pulmonary circulation oxygenates blood in the lungs, and systemic circulation delivers it to the tissues.
• In clotting, thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin.
• If a serum causes clumping, the red cells carry that antigen.
• Active immunity lasts, while passive immunity is fast but short-lived.
cards.15.svg#9: innate (same for all) + specific (antibodies, T cells, memory)
quiz.0.q: After a run, a person's pulse is 120 beats/min. How many seconds does one heart cycle take?
quiz.0.e: One minute is 60 seconds. 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 seconds. When the heart speeds up, the cycle gets shorter, and diastole shortens the most.
quiz.1.q: Match the serum results (+ clumping, − no clumping) with the blood type.
quiz.1.e: A serum with clumping shows that the red cells carry that antigen. Clumping in anti-A shows A, in anti-B shows B, and in anti-D shows the Rh (D) antigen. If there is no clumping in either anti-A or anti-B, the blood type is O.
quiz.2.q: Group each case by the type of immunity.
quiz.2.e: In active immunity, the body makes the antibodies itself. Getting a vaccine and having the disease are examples. In passive immunity, ready-made antibodies are received. Antiserum, antibodies from the mother through the placenta and milk, and the anti-D shot are examples.
quiz.3.q: Someone who has taken antibiotics for a long time has fewer gut bacteria and now lacks vitamin K. Which step of clotting is directly affected?
quiz.3.o.3: Absorbing Ca²⁺ ions from the intestine
quiz.3.e: The liver makes prothrombin using vitamin K. When prothrombin drops, less thrombin and therefore less fibrin form, and bleeding lasts longer.
quiz.3.y.0: Platelets do not depend on vitamin K. The plug forms, but the clot sets late.
quiz.3.y.2: The fibrin mesh is a later step. The real problem is that there is less thrombin to make fibrin.
quiz.3.y.3: Ca²⁺ absorption is increased by vitamin D, not vitamin K.
A:ozet: Send blood from the heart to the lungs and tissues, repair the valves, set the pulse, find matching blood and see on a graph why vaccines work.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The heart has valves that keep blood flowing in one direction. This heart's valves do not close fully. Press play and see what happens to the blood, then repair the valves.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.ipucu: When the ventricle contracts, the door to the atrium should close and the door to the aorta should open.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: When the ventricle contracted, the bicuspid valve closed and the semilunar valve opened. So all the blood went into the aorta. On the right side, the tricuspid valve does the same job.
A:adimlar.1.metin: At rest, one heart cycle takes 0.8 seconds. Set the pulse to match.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: One minute is 60 seconds. How many 0.8-second cycles fit into 60 seconds?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats/min. Even if the heart's nerves are cut, the heart keeps beating at this rhythm. The nerves only adjust its rate.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The right half of the heart pumps blood to the lungs, and the left half pumps it to the body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins bring it back. Make a guess first, then follow a drop of blood.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What is the blood in the pulmonary artery like?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: An artery is a vessel that carries blood away from the heart, and it does not have to be oxygenated. The blood going to the lungs has left its oxygen in the tissues.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The blood picks up O₂ in the lungs and returns oxygenated to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: In humans, the right and left halves of the heart are separate. So oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix.
A:adimlar.3.metin: When a tube of blood is spun, it separates into two parts. The yellowish plasma is on top, and the cells collect at the bottom. Look at each component one by one.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: In which part of blood are antibodies carried?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Red blood cells carry oxygen with hemoglobin. Their membranes carry the antigens that set the blood type, but they do not carry antibodies.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Antibodies are made by plasma cells that develop from B lymphocytes. But the released antibodies do not stay in the cell. They are carried dissolved in the plasma.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Plasma is about 55% of blood. It is mostly water, and it carries proteins such as albumin, fibrinogen and antibodies.
A:adimlar.4.metin: As blood moves from the aorta to the capillaries and then to the veins, its pressure and speed change. Pick each vessel and look at the graph.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: Why does blood flow slowest in the capillaries?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Their total cross section is largest
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A single capillary is very thin, but there are billions of them. So their total cross section is many times wider than the aorta. Blood spreads into a wide bed, slows down and has time for exchange.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: At the arterial end of a capillary, the pressure is still high enough to push fluid into the tissue. Pressure near zero is found in the vena cava.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: It is the opposite, because a capillary wall is one cell thick. The thin wall makes exchange easier.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Blood type is set by the antigens on red blood cells. Plasma holds antibodies against them. The recipient's blood type is O. Find a matching donor.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: Type O plasma has both anti-A and anti-B. Look for red cells with no antigen.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: Only type O red cells did not clump, because they have no A or B antigen on their membranes. That is why type O is the universal donor. If it is Rh−, it also matches everyone for Rh. Still, a compatibility test is always done before a transfusion.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A vaccine introduces the body to an antigen that does not cause disease. Make a guess first, then watch the antibody graph.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: What is the antibody response like at the second contact with the same antigen?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Memory cells remain after the first contact. Because the body recognizes the antigen, the response is not the same.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The body does not get used to the antigen and weaken its response. Memory cells make the response faster instead.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Memory cells multiply right away, and antibodies rise to a much higher level in a short time. The microbe is stopped before it can cause disease. This is why active immunity lasts long.
A:kapanis.0: In pulmonary circulation blood picks up oxygen in the lungs, and in systemic circulation it delivers this oxygen to the tissues. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
A:kapanis.1: Valves keep blood flowing in one direction. At rest, one heart cycle takes 0.8 seconds, which is 75 beats per minute.
A:kapanis.2: Plasma makes up 55% of blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells defend the body, and platelets start clotting.
A:kapanis.3: Blood pressure falls from the aorta toward the veins. Blood flows slowest in the capillaries, which have the widest total cross section.
A:kapanis.4: If an antigen on red cells meets the recipient's antibody, clumping occurs. A vaccine leaves memory cells, so the second response is fast and strong.
